A motion was duly made, seconded, and passed that the report of the

It was duly moved (General Resolution No. 1) that the aforementioned
proposed amendment be adopted, subject to the approval of the Chapters,

Twenty-four Chapters voted "aye," in
Convention. Delegates of three were absent. Iota, Phi, Beta Beta. The
motion was passed. The amended Section 6 of Article II of the Constitu
tion, as approved by the Convention, reads in full as follows :
Article II, Section 6 : The Convention held in the year 1908 shall
elect an Executive Council of ten, a majority of whom shall be graduate
members of the Fraternity and no more than two from the same
Chapter. The said Council, at its first meeting after its election shall
divide itself by lot into five classes of two members each, whose respec
tive terms of office shall be one, two, three, four and five years. There
after, the convention shall annually elect two members to replace the
outgoing class and to serve for five years each.
Commencing with the Convention held in April 1932, each Conven
tion shall elect, for a five year term, one additional member to the
Executive Council, until its membership shall have been increased to
fifteen, and thereafter three members shall be elected annually to fill
the vacancies caused by the expiration of terms. (Resolution No. 1,
Convention Records 1932, page 6).
The headquarters of the Council shall be in the City of New York.
The Council shall elect a President, a Secretary and Treasurer, shall reg
ulate its own proceedings and assignments of duty and shall be empow
ered to employ a member of the Fraternity to act as Assistant Secretary,
and who shall receive therefor such compensation as shall be authorized
by the Convention. The Council shall issue calls and make all arrange
ments for special conventions when requested so to do, in writing by
at least five Chapters; shall give official announcements of the passage
of any measure requiring the consent of the Chapters; shall keep the
Fraternity seal, all Fraternity property, the official copy of the Consti
tution and Convention records, a copy of the laws of each Chapter and
as complete statistics of them as possible. It shall have power under
the regulation of the Convention to make and collect assessments on
the several Chapters in proportion to the number of members in each;
shall allow claims against the Fraternity; shall superintend the publi
cation of Fraternity documents ; shall decide all points at issue between
Chapters when appealed to. The Council shall fill its own vacancies
and shall submit annually to the Convention a communication embracing
a report of its transactions with such recommendations as to the affairs
of the Fraternity as it may deem proper. The Council may investigate
applications for charters of the Fraternity and, upon its own motion,
may inquire into the expediency of establishing a Chapter at any college
or university. Within thirty days after the close of any such investi-

gation or inquiry, the Council shall transmit to each Chapter or to the

shall, at regular periods, cause the Chapters to be visited by one or

funds to be specially contributed or otherwise provided for that pur
pose. The contents of any report on such visitation shall be communi

President Stevens broached the subject of "Hell Week" for informal
discussion. The following Brothers spoke: Brothers Hart, Xi 32; Spooner,
Rho '94; Stevens, Chi '99; and delegates from the Tau, Eta, Psi, Delta,
Theta Theta, Nu, and Beta Chapters, and Brother Corcoran, Omega '15.
Brother Stevens, Chi '99, summed up the discussion, mentioning the follow
ing points: that "Hell Week" should not include anything which might
violate the Fraternity's attitude of friendship or which might violate good
taste, that it should be run with consideration for privacy and under super
vision of upperclassmen rather than sophomores, and that treatment of
candidates should be varied according to the physical and mental peculiari
ties of the individual.

Resolution No. 10. Resolved:
Section 1. That there shall be organized a National Rushing Com
mittee under the direction of a member of the Executive Council and
whose members shall be appointed by the Executive Council. It is
suggested that the Committee be composed in part of the Junior
members of the rushing committees of the individual Chapters.
Section 2. It is suggested that among the duties of this body
shall be:
A. To aid the Chapters as far as possible in their sub-freshman
rushing by
1. Securing the assistance and co-operation of the alumni in all
sections of the country for
rushing.
2. By contacting the Psi Upsilon members on the
faculty and
among the recent alumni of the various preparatory schools in
order to find out and advise the Chapters which desirable sub-
freshmen propose to attend their respective colleges.
3. To serve as a clearing house for recommendations for mem

bership.
4. To keep in touch with the rushing systems and the
systems of
pledging in the various colleges where there are Chapters of the
Fraternity, and to forward the recommendations of rushees to
the various Chapters in time for them to take the best
advantage
according to their systems.

forms to contain the items of social standing, financial situation,

and the rushing chairman of any Chapter when the latter desires

Resolution No. 11. Resolved: That the Convention in the 99th

of them working in conjunction with their Alumni Associations, in

1932 Convention of the Fraternity, in an endeavor to raise their scholar

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
OF THE
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL OF PSI UPSILON
TO THE 1932 CONVENTION OF THE FRATERNITY,
HELD WITH THE DELTA CHAPTER,
APRIL 7, 8 and 9, 1932

In June, eighteen hundred and forty, before Psi Upsilon had completed
her seventh year, undergraduates from our first four Chapters gathered
together in New Haven for the first Convention of our Fraternity; and, in
the year following, the old Deha Chapter again brought together the dele
gates from those same four early Chapters, this time in New York City.
The next year apparently, no meeting of our Chapters was held; but in 1843
Psi Upsilon's third Convention met at the home of the Theta. Since that
time, no year except 1918 has passed without an annual Convention of
undergraduate representatives from our slowly growing hst of Chapters;
and now our Delta Chapter, for the fifth time in its long history of more
than ninety-five years, is once again our gracious host.
It is twenty years since the last previous Convention, that with the
Lambda, was held in New York City; and twenty-five years since the last
previous Convention with the Delta. Alumni attendance and interest fea
tured both of those Conventions; and we hope that the same will be true
again this year, especially in view of the fact that on the last afternoon of
this Convention, Saturday, April 9th, an alumni meeting is to be
held, at
which the Executive Council will submit a comprehensive plan for the
national organization of our alumni, to carry out the instructions
given by
the 1931 Convention.
Vote on Petitions: By resolution of the 1931
Convention, the petitions
of "The Wranglers" of Northwestern University and of the Alpha
Kappa
Alpha Fraternity of the University of British Columbia were submitted to
the Chapters of our Fraternity for appropriate action, with the instruction
that such action be taken and reported to the Executive Council
before the

"Hell Week": In spite of the resolutions passed by the 1929 and 1930
Conventions, a few complaints have been made to the Executive Council by
college authorities, and some of our alumni, as to the pre-initiation activities
in some Chapters. We are confident that, in general, the abuse and over
emphasis of "Hell Week" have been to a large extent done away with by
our Chapters, but, in view of these complaints, we deem it advisable to

repeat what we said in our annual communication to the 1929 Convention
held in Washington, D. C, viz. :
Preparation of Undergraduates for Initiation : "Hell Week" Our Chap

ters have always recognized the vital need of preparing their pledges for
initiation by systematic instruction in the Fraternity's songs, history, organi
zation, traditions and ideals; and most of them have added some short
probationary disciplinary prelude, to impress upon the initiates the great sig
nificance and lifelong duration of the fraternal bonds they were about to
assume. The basic purpose of these preparations is to open the eyes of the
pledges to our Fraternity's honored past, to start them in the right way
toward an understanding of its time-tested ideals and to lead them into such
an attitude of mind and spirit that they will appreciate fully our beautiful

initiation ritual and all that it implies. To this end, many of our Chapters
have devised preliminary rituals, planned to bring about a closer personal
contact with the individual initiates and to impress more intensely on each
of them those fundamental facts and ideas. With all this the Council
sympathizes entirely. These preparatory ceremonies are often of real value.
They have given an opportunity for original and creative contributions to
our local traditions and have helped to individualize the Chapters. But
occasionally, both in the past and in recent years, changes have crept in
changes which have sometimes had a distinct tendency not only
to arouse
the criticism and opposition of college authorities, but also to subvert the
real purpose of the pre-initiation instruction and probation and to
cheapen
the constitutional ritual itself. College administrations rightly
oppose and
we believe, will soon prohibit all "rough-house,"
vulgar, indecent, exhaust
ing and dangerous tests and practices and also all demands on candidates
which in any way tend to interfere with their regular study hours and

college duties. While many, perhaps most, of our Chapters are entirely
free from the practices which have been criticized, we have noted a growing
tendency to include "rough-house" in some form and also a physical exhaus
tion of initiates, in several of our Chapters. We agree with the college
authorities in opposing such practices; but we go further. We feel deeply
that all preliminary treatment of initiates should be in strict keeping with
that spirit of fraternal friendship which is our Fraternity's foundation and
with the expression of that spirit which comes so vividly before our initi
ates as the climax of their induction into Psi U 
our constitutional ritual.
Surely, no member of our Fraternity would consciously let the practices of
the old-fashioned "high school frat" mingle impressions with the inspired
language of that ritual of ours, nor would he let silly and often harmful
practices color the minds of the initiates at that moment of keenest impres
sions and cause them honestly to wonder, contrasting the rough and farcical
preliminary initiation with the solemn one which follows, which is the sham ?
Most of our initiates today are thinking and reflecting human beings ; and
we must not be surprised if, with growing frequency, they show that they

cannot reconcile cruel paddling and dangerous exposure with the expressions
of fraternal affection. Such practices are potentially as dangerous to the
spirit of our initiates as to their bodies. We believe that proper preparation
is essential, but that Hell Week is entirely wrong.
The Centennial: November 24, 1933 will be a gala day for all mem

bers of Psi Upsilon for on that day we will celebrate the 100th birthday

of our founding. It is to be expected that the greatest gathering in our
history will occur on this memorable day when the legions of Psi Upsilon
will meet at Schenectady, New York, with our Mother Chapter, the Theta,
at old Union College.

It is the recommendation of the Executive Council that this Convention
authorize the 1933 Convention to be held with the Theta Chapter on Novem
ber 23, 24 and 25 as per their invitation. This will necessitate the elimina
tion of the usual Convention in April of 1933.
It is but fitting that a Committee of the Whole or a Committee of
14,000 should be authorized by this Convention to be the Committee of the
Centennial. Every living member of the Fraternity should feel that he is
a member of the Committee and do his part to participate in the festivities.

Since 1924 our undergraduateChapters have been gathering a Centen
nial fund by a tax of $2.00 per year per man; the Executive Council now
has this money on hand, a fund of $14,200. Surely our thousands of
alumni will wish to give their mite toward this fund so that we may
celebrate our Centennial in an appropriate manner. In addition to the
private exercises during the three days of the Centennial Convention, the
proper public exercises should be held so that the world may know our joy
at reaching our 100th anniversary. We should erect at Union College some
mark of our affection for the place where Psi Upsilon was born and it

Amendment to the Constitution : For some period of time the
Council has felt that, due to the gradual growth of our Chapter roll since
1908 when the size of the Council was increased from five to ten, it is
advisable that we gradually add more alumni to the Council so as to increase
its membership to fifteen alumni. With the addition of five Chapters since
1908, we feel the need of wider representation on the Council, and, more
important still, of allowing more alumni an opportunity of serving Psi
Upsilon. We are also desirous of bringing into the Council some younger
brothers, so that we may not lose contact with the undergraduate point of
view of today and at the same time may maintain on the Council older
brothers more familiar with our Fraternity's history and problems.
